input: A staffing review has been carried out for the dispatch office, and this passage summarises the current position and the option under consideration. The office currently operates with 15 full-time staff, and over the course of last year overtime accounted for 14% of paid hours, which represents a substantial and ongoing commitment. One option that has been identified is to replace half of the overtime with one additional hire, and it has been estimated that a hire would cost $82k per year on a fully loaded basis. It is important to note, however, that the overtime is not spread evenly across the year: it is concentrated in two seasonal peaks, whereas a hire is paid for the full year, including the quieter periods in between. This means that the $82k per year cost of the hire is fixed and continuous, while the overtime it would replace is intermittent. At the peaks themselves, it should also be appreciated that only half of the overtime working would be replaced, and the remainder would continue as before, so the peaks would still place considerable demands on the existing team. Overall, the decision is not simply a comparison of costs, and a range of operational factors, including the question of cover outside the peaks and the resilience of the office during busy periods, would also need to be taken into account before any change is made. The review therefore presents the option and the figures behind it, and leaves the decision to be taken once those wider considerations have been worked through.
target: Replace half of the dispatch office overtime with one additional hire. The office manager owns the change. The office ran 15 full-time staff last year, and overtime took 14% of paid hours (payroll record for the year). A hire costs $82k per year fully loaded and replaces half of that overtime. The trade-off stands in one sentence: the hire costs $82k in every week of the year, while the overtime it replaces falls in two seasonal peaks. Outside the peaks the hire is paid at the same rate and the replaced overtime does not arise. At the peaks the change is narrower than the headline suggests: half of the peak overtime is replaced by rostered hours, and the other half of the overtime working at the peaks is untouched. The evidence base is the payroll record for one year. That record shows the hours and their distribution, and the two peaks stand in it as the periods where overtime concentrates; it says nothing about a year in which the peaks move or grow, and a different peak pattern changes the balance of the trade-off. The cost side of the decision is fixed by the figures above. The cover side is not in the figures: outside the peaks the hire is present and rostered, where the present arrangement offers only the overtime that happens to be worked. Next step: the office manager sets the hire against the roster for the two peaks and reports the cover outside the peaks before the decision is taken.
